title: AI in Our Schools—Its Use and Abuse
author: Larry Sand
summary: Retired California teacher Larry Sand argues that AI cheating is now widespread and that schools must respond by shifting toward in-person assessment. He cites a Fordham Institute paper reporting that large shares of students use AI to solve math problems, avoid reading and draft essays, and that most agree AI makes homework meaningless. He then turns to the 2025 PISA results, where the OECD found that students who regularly use AI scored significantly worse, and the United States fell in reading. His proposals are more frequent in-person tests with greater weight, state exams two or three times a year as Neetu Arnold suggests, and college blue-book, oral and chalkboard assessments in place of take-home exams. He highlights Case Western's blue book surge, a Bucknell professor's no-technology rule and the University of Chicago's plan to teach students to think with and without machines. He concludes that AI is not going away and, like cars, needs limits and serious discussion about children.
points: Surveys cited in the piece show students using AI to solve math, summarize assigned reading and draft essays, with most agreeing it has made homework meaningless.
PISA 2025 results indicate that frequent AI users scored significantly lower, and the OECD links more screen time and hasty reading to weaker results.
Sand proposes weighting in-person assessments more heavily and treating AI-assisted homework as practice rather than grade material.
Colleges are already reverting to blue books, oral exams and handwritten work, and some professors ban technology in class entirely.
The author compares AI to cars, which could not be uninvented but were limited by age rules, speed limits and insurance.
quotes: When asked to respond to statements about AI’s effects on school, 58% of students agree that it has made homework meaningless, and 57% agree that it lets students get good grades without doing real work.
The OECD data pointed to an obvious culprit behind this alarming trend—students who regularly use AI scored significantly worse on the tests than those who don’t.
To combat this disturbing trend, K-12 schools need to take in-person assessments more seriously. This could include administering more frequent tests and giving them greater weight in final grades.

Colleges should also adopt a different approach to assessing students. Take-home exams should be eliminated. Instead, schools should administer in-class evaluations, such as blue-book essays, oral exams, and chalkboard demonstrations.
According to Walt Hunter, a humanities professor at Case Western Reserve University, blue book sales have surged at his school.

The first goal is that our students should learn, during their time with us, to be ethical, skeptical, and ambitious about the role of AI in their education and their lives. The second is that all students at UChicago should learn to think both with and without machines.
The same is true for AI. It isn’t going away, so we must have a serious discussion about how to address its reality—especially as it relates to children—and do so immediately.
